newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Exiled China dissident seeks to visit Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: Exiled China dissident seeks to visit Taiwan.

text.p: Exiled Chinese dissident Wang Xizhe has applied to visit Taiwan, where he has raised eyebrows by expressing a desire to join the ruling Nationalist Party that was defeated by China's communists in 1949.

Wang, a longtime activist who fled the mainland in October as Beijing was putting fellow dissidents on trial, requested permission from Taiwan's Mainland Affairs Council to visit from his temporary U.S. base, a council spokesman said on Tuesday.
"He can come if he meets our regulations," the spokesman said without disclosing details of Wang's letter.

Wang, 46, slipped out of China's Guangdong province just days after Beijing authorities ordered fellow democracy advocate Liu Xiaobo to serve three years' hard labour. Activist Wang Dan was imprisoned for 11 years for subversion a few weeks later.

Wang Xizhe emerged in the United States but vowed not to seek U.S. political asylum until Taiwan said whether he was welcome on the island, which is seen by China as a renegade province since the defeated Chinese Nationalists took refuge there in 1949.
Under Taiwan law, mainland citizens can apply to visit on a case-by-case basis. Those with demonstrable contributions to democracy can migrate to Taiwan.
"If he wants to immigrate to Taiwan, which we don't know yet, we will review his qualifications according to our law," the council official said.

Taiwan's United Daily News, reporting from New York, quoted Wang's letter to council chairman Chang King-yuh as pledging to learn more about Taiwan and to help clear up some "unrealistic" impressions of China's communists.

Wang surprised many exiled Chinese dissidents by saying that he hoped to join the Nationalist Party so he could speak for Taipei in negotiations with the Chinese Communist Party over Taiwan's possible reunification with the mainland.

Some exiled activists, in articles and television appearances, have suggested Wang had little understanding of the Nationalists, whose Cold War-era "recover the mainland" policies have long given way to a focus on building Taiwan's democracy with only a cautious policy on unification.
In his letter, Wang professed love for "this beautiful piece of the motherland" but said he wanted to see Taiwan's democracy for himself before deciding whether to join the party.
The Nationalist Party has said it would welcome Wang if he identified himself with Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government and its policies.
Though both governments say they want reunification, Taiwan maintains this is not possible before China adopts pluralist democratic reforms like those it has embraced since 1987.

Wang's activism dates to 1974 when he co-wrote an attack on the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution. He took part in the 1979 Democracy Wall movement in Beijing and produced his own dissident newsletters.
He was twice imprisoned, spending 17 years in prison and labour camps. He was paroled in 1993.
